speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: asked the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance of the estimated more than 60% of net GST that is accounted for by foreigners residing in Singapore, tourists and the top 20% of resident households, what is the share paid by each group.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: asked the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance between 2016 and 2021, what is the Ministry's estimate on the proportion and amount of GST revenue that are paid by non-residents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: asked the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance how much has the Tourism Refund Scheme paid out in GST refunds for tourists between 2010 and 2021.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have not used data for 2020 and 2021, as they are not representative of general consumption patterns due to the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The first is, I am wondering whether the benefit of the additional revenue gain from an estimated, as he had shared, 50% drawn from foreigners and non-residents may actually be worth the additional pain that our middle class will need to endure?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I speak especially for our sandwich generation in my constituency of Sengkang, where households who earn sufficiently high incomes nevertheless receive limited support, in terms of support programmes from the Government and continue to face high expenses supporting their children and parents, which will now be subject to a higher GST.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My second question has to do with whether the Ministry has also studied the incidence of the tax.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Because, as we know, the burden need not fall on the party which the tax is levied on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To put it another way, the higher GST charges may well crimp demand at the margin, and this may result in Singaporean businesses bearing the burden of reduced demand and hence, lower profits, rather than foreigners paying more, even if it looks like the revenue comes from foreigners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Does the MOF have any estimates of the relative share of GST that will be paid for explicitly by foreign consumers versus local businesses?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: What this means is that the remaining 30% is spread over the rest of the 80% of households and individuals.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, yes, there will certainly be some part of the net GST that is paid for by different groups of society, different income quintiles, including the middle-income and the upper middle-income.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, if you look at the middle 40th to 60th, and also the 60th to the 80th, certainly, I think they do bear some of the GST.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But the impact of the GST that they bear is not the full amount.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In addition to that, Sir, we have also shared earlier that we provide support, to include the middle-income households.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, the support that goes to lower-income households is a lot more because they are more vulnerable and they are more affected by price increases.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But in designing the support packages, what was announced in Budget this year and the two packages of $1.5 billion each, we did not leave out the middle-income.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In fact, part of those packages included the middle-income.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And there were some parts of the support package that were not means-tested.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: All were designed such that people who stay in private properties or who earn higher incomes – those who I believe would belong to the middle class and upper-middle class that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim spoke about – they would also be included.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For example, the special payment that would be given out in December this year, 2.5 million Singaporeans will benefit.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, what I shared with Assoc Prof Jamus Lim earlier were based on what we had actually collected in 2018 and 2019.
